Bigtooth corvina (Isopisthus parvipinnis) attains a maximum recorded total length of 41.5 centimeters [Li = 41.5 centimeters], a value that places it among the smaller members of the family Sciaenidae found in the eastern Pacific. Field surveys along the coasts of Ecuador and Peru indicate that individuals rarely exceed this asymptotic size, with growth trajectories decelerating markedly after the onset of reproductive activity. The species demonstrates a moderately rapid growth rate during its first two years of life, during which most of the ultimate body mass is accumulated. The corresponding ultimate wet weight has been estimated at 737 grams [Wwi = 737 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from local fishery landings, a figure consistent with the general body plan of a slender, fast-swimming predator adapted to shallow, turbid waters. This relatively modest body size is thought to reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the warm, productive upwelling habitats it frequents, where abundant prey are available but competition among sciaenids is intense. Seasonal variations in condition factor suggest that peak somatic growth occurs during the warmest months when prey densities are highest.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, females typically measure 15.9 centimeters [Lp = 15.9 centimeters] in total length, a stage that corresponds to approximately 38.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 38.7 grams] of wet weight. This length at puberty represents roughly 38 percent of the ultimate total length, a relatively early maturation schedule compared to larger, more fecund congeneric species such as Cynoscion guatucupa, which delays reproduction until a larger body size is attained. The relationship between body length and mass at this life stage follows the same allometric equation derived for adults, indicating that the transition to reproductive status is not accompanied by a major shift in body shape or condition. Field collections of gravid females suggest that first spawning events occur soon after the attainment of this size threshold, typically during the late spring and early summer months when water temperatures are rising and planktonic food resources for larvae are most abundant. Historical records from the Gulf of Guayaquil indicate that females may undergo their first reproductive event as early as their second year of life, though this timing can vary with local environmental conditions and individual growth rates.

Newly fertilized eggs of Bigtooth corvina are characterized by a mean diameter of approximately 0.6 millimeters, which translates into an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.0001 grams [Wwb = 0.0001 grams] for the developing embryo within the chorion. This minute mass is typical of pelagic sciaenid eggs that are released directly into the water column, where they undergo rapid development sustained entirely by endogenous yolk reserves. Incubation periods are short, generally lasting between 18 and 24 hours at the prevailing water temperatures of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] commonly encountered in the species' spawning grounds along the continental shelf. The small egg size and rapid embryonic development are consistent with an r-selected reproductive strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring investment, a pattern common among marine fishes inhabiting variable coastal environments. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larvae measure roughly 1.2 millimeters in total length and remain in a non-feeding state for an additional two to three days while completing the absorption of their remaining yolk reserves and the differentiation of their digestive systems.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been reported at approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%] for this species under the thermal conditions typical of its spawning season at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. Histological examination of ovarian tissue has confirmed the presence of oocytes at multiple developmental stages simultaneously, providing direct evidence for batch spawning and underscoring the species' capacity for protracted reproductive output.

Maximum documented longevity for Bigtooth corvina in the eastern Pacific is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a lifespan that is relatively extended for a sciaenid of its body size when considered at the species' typical thermal regime of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. This age estimate, derived from otolith increment analysis of individuals captured in artisanal fisheries off the coast of Ecuador, indicates a slow pace of senescence that is somewhat unusual among fast-growing, early-maturing scianids from tropical waters. The relationship between body size and lifespan in this species conforms broadly to the pattern observed across the Sciaenidae, wherein maximum longevity tends to increase with asymptotic length, though Isopisthus parvipinnis lives longer than would be predicted solely from its ultimate length of 41.5 centimeters [Li = 41.5 centimeters]. This extended lifespan may be linked to the relatively stable, productive upwelling habitat it occupies, where food availability remains high throughout the year and mortality from predation is moderate. The demographic data further suggest that the species maintains a balanced population structure with multiple age classes present in the spawning stock, a characteristic that confers resilience to moderate levels of fishing pressure.
